item.title: The Last High School Football Team in Town
item.description:
The night before one of the biggest games of the season, Doug Hogue had gathered his team in the cafeteria of Roosevelt High School in Yonkers, N.Y. He told them to remember where to line up before each snap, to play with passion and avoid mistakes — the usual coach talk.

He also reminded them about the unusual compromise they had made to keep their program alive. Before the season started, Yonkers merged its two remaining high school football teams in a last-ditch effort to avoid the fate of other schools across the country that canceled their seasons because they did not have enough players.

The school district named Mr. Hogue, a former N.F.L. player who grew up in Yonkers, as head coach of the new hybrid team, the Yonkers Guardians. Some players had opposed the merger, worried they might not get along with their former crosstown rivals. Others figured it was their only option if they wanted to play football.

“We wanted a chance to have a senior season,” said Omar Areche, 17, a wide receiver who tried to convince his teammates that the plan made sense.

The experiment had been a series of highs and lows, with dominant wins at home and heartbreaking losses on the road. But in mid-October, with two games left in the regular season, the Guardians still had a shot at the playoffs.

“To come together and try to figure this out wasn’t easy,” Mr. Hogue told the players over a team dinner of pizza and pasta. “Some of you guys were with it. Some of you guys weren’t. But you made it happen. And now you are setting the foundation for something.”

Yonkers, the third largest city in New York state, had eight varsity football teams just a decade ago, one for each public high school. Now it is down to one. A diverse, working-class suburb on the northern edge of New York City, it is known for having an underfunded school system and a long history of racially segregated public housing.

Last Saturday, the Guardians faced the Mamaroneck Tigers as heavy underdogs with a 2-3 record. Mamaroneck, an affluent town 10 miles to the east, had their own cheerleaders. Yonkers did not. But the Guardians had hundreds of enthusiastic fans in the stands, rooting for them and waving posters with the players’ faces.

With about a minute left in the fourth quarter, the Guardians had a 12-0 lead. Their quarterback, Brendan Mulvihill, took the snap and, narrowly avoiding a sack, threw a deep pass down the sideline to Omar, who raced for a first down and deep into Tigers territory, sealing the victory. The players celebrated by sprinting across the field carrying a giant white flag with the team’s helmet logo.

Inside the locker room, the players took a knee as Mr. Hogue spoke.

“All season we’ve been beating ourselves, and we finally put it together,” he said.

For their final game, the Guardians traveled yesterday to a Hudson Valley village called Wappingers Falls to play Roy C. Ketcham High School. After mounting a furious comeback, Yonkers fell to Ketcham, 29-26. Whether the Guardians get into the playoffs now depends on the results of other games.

Across the state, high school football teams are fighting for survival. At least seven New York high schools, including four on Long Island, have canceled their varsity football seasons this year because they didn’t have enough players. Football is still America’s most popular boys’ sport. More than one million teenagers played last year, according to the National Federation of State High School Associations, which oversees high school athletics.

But over the past decade, the United States has lost about 40,000 players. Some high schools have addressed the decline in participation by playing games with six or eight players on the field instead of 11.

But the fact remains that full-contact football is now seen as a dangerous sport. Flag football has taken off as a safer alternative, and it will be an official Olympic sport for the first time at the Summer Games in Los Angeles in 2028.

On a recent evening in Yonkers, dozens of children, ranging from 9 to 14 years old, played in a flag football league, sprinting across Coyne Park with yellow flags dangling from their belts.

From the sidelines of one flag football game, Nick DeMatteis, 50, a high school teacher in New York City, watched his 11-year-old son Billy. Mr. DeMatteis grew up playing full-contact football, and he believes that the chronic migraines he has experienced are from football-related concussions he suffered as a boy.

“His brain is not turning into mashed potatoes while we’re playing this game,” Mr. DeMatteis said, gesturing toward his son.

Often teenagers are motivated to play traditional football by having the right coach, said Davis Whitfield, the federation’s chief executive officer.

“Sometimes you have a special coach walking the halls that gets kids excited about playing,” he said.

For decades, Yonkers had Coach Tony DeMatteo, who led Roosevelt High School to seven undefeated seasons, including the only state football championship in Yonkers history. In 2000, Mr. DeMatteo left to coach at a high school outside the city, and that was the start of a steady decline in Yonkers football. Many talented prospects left for stronger programs.

“The private schools and the Catholic schools come in there and take all the good players away,” Mr. DeMatteo, who retired from full-time coaching in 2021, said in an interview. “That really hurts Yonkers.”

In 2018, facing smaller rosters as well as rising financial pressures, the Yonkers school officials condensed the eight high school programs into two teams, the Force and the Brave.

Then, in a meeting at the Roosevelt High cafeteria in June, Yonkers officials gathered players from the two remaining teams to see how they felt about merging into one. The Force had won the last five games between the two teams, but they still had a heated rivalry.

Each player got a turn at the microphone to sound off. Gabriel Concepcion, a rising senior, argued that the merger could make the combined team more competitive. “We could go on a playoff run and hopefully win a championship if we all merge our talent together,” he said.

Mickey Salvato, 17, a linebacker for the Brave, was against the merger. “The Force players thought they were better than us,” he said recently. “There were a lot of egos and different personalities. I couldn’t see it happening.”

At first, it didn’t go smoothly. The Guardians began the season with nearly 100 varsity players. They disagreed over which team’s playbook to use. Some picked lockers next to their former teammates.

“It was very cliquey,” said Brendan, the quarterback who had played for the Force. “We had all these petty arguments.” Several players quit because they worried they weren’t going to get playing time with fewer available spots, and by mid-October, the roster had shrunk to about 40 players.

The new coach, Mr. Hogue, wanted to find a way to win, something that has been a challenge in Yonkers since his playing days. During his senior season at Roosevelt High School, the team was 1-7. Still, he was a standout. He went on to play at Syracuse University and then made it to the N.F.L. for a couple of seasons, playing for the Detroit Lions and the Carolina Panthers.

After leaving professional football, he decided to get a degree in physical education and return to Yonkers. He started a foundation with his sister, a former Yonkers basketball star, that offers free tutoring and takes local high school students to visit colleges. “I felt I could give so much more to the kids who come from where I come from, who went through the same struggles as I did,” he said. When the school district asked him to help the football program, he accepted.

As the head coach of the merged team, Mr. Hogue knew that his first obstacle would be getting the new team to bond. He took them to a New York Giants preseason game at MetLife Stadium in August.

He held a ceremony around a fire pit where he gave each player a piece of paper and some instructions. On one side, he said, describe how you portray yourself. Many wrote that they hoped to appear “tough” or “happy.” On the other side, he asked them to describe how they felt inside. Some shared that they were “depressed” or “not good enough.”

They read the words aloud then crumpled up the papers and threw them in the fire. The point of the exercise, Mr. Hogue said, “is to realize that everybody is in the same boat.”

The fire pit ceremony seemed to work. “Everybody got a little vulnerable,” he said. “We talked about starting anew. Ever since that day, everybody has bought in.”

A bigger question is whether Yonkers football can survive past this season. Mr. Hogue needs to build a pipeline of fresh talent, but parents’ fears over concussions has made it harder to attract players, he said. But for some teenagers, football can be a ticket out of Yonkers. For others, it offers a mental break.

“This is an escape from some of their living conditions, an escape from what might be stressing them out at home, an escape from the pressure they go through in school,” Mr. Hogue said. “Some of these kids are depressed. Coming here is an outlet where they can just be themselves.”

Brendan, now a senior, quit football during his freshman year because he felt he wasn’t good enough. Now he’s one of the team’s stars.

“When there’s a lot of stuff going on at home or off the field, I take all that and put it on the field,” he said.

Brendan’s father works for the Metro-North Railroad. His mother is in the army. Neither went to college. He hopes to play football in college next year and someday at the professional level. Mr. Hogue is a role model.

“He went to the N.F.L. from Yonkers,” Brendan said. “If he did it, why can’t I?”

item.title: What Are the Best Ways to Fix Schools?
item.description:
To the Editor:

Re “Top Ideas for Fixing Schools, Ranked by the Experts” (The Upshot, Oct. 7):

I have spent 15 years working with schools, nonprofits and foundations on how to improve education outcomes, particularly for young people growing up far from opportunity.

Your article lands on an important conclusion: No single intervention is enough, context matters, and even good ideas depend heavily on implementation.

But ranking 30 interventions by effectiveness and cost still feeds one of education’s most persistent bad habits: the search for a silver bullet.

The cycle is familiar. Poor results create urgency. We ask what works quickly, cheaply and at scale. We identify a promising intervention, implement it unevenly, become disappointed when it falls short and move on.

The problem is not that we lack promising ideas. It is that we keep asking them to work for many different students and in many different contexts, quickly and affordably. Little meets those criteria in any field, much less amid the profound complexities that Nikole Hannah-Jones brought to life in her Oct. 4 New York Times Magazine article about choosing schools for her daughter, Najya.

Instead of asking which intervention will fix education, school leaders might start with a more useful question: What experience do our students need, and how do we align our time, people and resources around delivering it well?

Rob JentschBaltimore

To the Editor:

It’s remarkable to read 30 ideas for fixing schools and find that not one involved asking the real experts: the students. The article emphasizes the need for quality of implementation for any idea. This depends not on outside experts or the administration but on those most directly involved: teachers and students.

My research and school reform work with thousands of students have generated a top 10 list of student priorities. Effective results can happen when we partner with students in pressing for change and work with them rather than for them.

Rick GordonJackson, Wyo.The writer is working with three colleagues on a book, “10,000 Student Voices: Transforming Schools Together.”

To the Editor:

If you look at a school like a business long enough, you start to see everything through that lens. Test scores become the product, teachers become inputs, and students become something to be measured and improved.

That is the logic behind “Top Ideas for Fixing Schools, Ranked by the Experts.” The article asks researchers to rank reforms by their effect on academic achievement, usually measured by standardized tests and by cost. From there, school accountability (rating schools) emerges as one of the best values.

But such conclusions depend on a very narrow idea of what schools are for. They reflect the same logic of efficiency, competition and measurable outcomes that has shaped decades of failed so-called reforms, including school-choice policies.

In my more than 20 years as a high school teacher and during my doctoral work in education, I have learned to take research seriously without mistaking it for a single settled story. For example, National Research Council research found that test-based incentive systems often produced small or effectively zero gains.

We should expect more from schools than higher scores at lower cost. We should care about whether young people are prepared to meet the needs of an ailing and troubled world marked by real challenges that extend far beyond a score on a standardized test.

Alex BernsteinChicago

To the Editor:

None of the ideas in this article address the orthodoxy of grade grouping by chronological age, which was started in the 19th century. From the beginning, critics observed that not all students fit their grade. Age grading is the Procrustean bed that causes problems for the less mature as well as the more precocious students in every grade. Age grading is a habit stronger than reason, as George Santayana would say.

Charles H. HargisKnoxville, Tenn.

To the Editor:

As a founder of a mental health nonprofit and a public-school teacher for more than a decade, I was disheartened that researchers and academics underestimated the importance of mental health for student achievement.

A mountain of studies shows that when young people have mental health issues, they can’t engage in school and have greater absenteeism compared with their peers. Worse, students report alarming rates of hopelessness, and suicide is the second-leading cause of death for young people ages 10 to 24.

On the flip side, research shows that early mental health intervention has lifelong benefits, like more educational attainment and greater lifetime earnings.

Schools must be part of a broader system that fosters well-being, preparing educators to identify mental health and addiction issues.

Amy KennedyBrigantine, N.J.

To the Editor:

Let’s not kid ourselves that fixing education in this country is as simple as throwing more money at it, or coming up with new approaches like frequent small-group tutoring.

Fixing education has to begin at home.

The root problem is our fundamental cultural lack of respect for education. Do children in this country go to school with the expectation that they will apply themselves to do their very best every day? A resounding no! The preoccupation with cellphones and social media while in school is symptomatic.

Do students even go to school with the expectation that they will respect their teachers and behave as if they are grateful to be offered a publicly funded education? Unfortunately, it’s the opposite.

Let’s contrast that with Malala Yousafzai, the Nobel Peace Prize-winning Pakistani girl who risked her life every day to attend school. After recovering from being shot in the head on the bus home from school, she said in an interview: “In some parts of the world, students are going to school every day. It’s their normal life. But in other parts of the world, we are starving for education … it’s like a precious gift. It’s like a diamond.”

How many American children consider public education a “precious gift”?

That’s what needs fixing.

Phoebe HuangStonington, Conn.

item.title: ‘Everything We Love Is on the Line’
item.description:
America’s midterm elections will probably be determined primarily by issues like affordability. But what is at stake goes far beyond the quotidian concerns that many voters are focused on.

The principles and strategies that over multiple generations have made the United States the world’s leading nation in effect are on the ballot, and these midterms mark a potential turning point.

Let’s focus on three pillars that explain the rise, strength and resilience of our nation.

First is education: The United States pioneered mass education in the 19th century and today operates great universities and research institutions that are among the nation’s crown jewels. These have given us an edge in the global economic competition. Yet President Trump, with the acquiescence of congressional Republicans, is vandalizing education, from Head Start for 4-year-olds living in poverty to elite universities researching new treatments for cancer.

Trump is trying to dismantle the Department of Education, cut student aid and slash support for the National Science Foundation and the National Institutes of Health. His war on America’s leading universities is particularly alarming, for he has variously attempted to defund them, cancel their tax-exempt status and make it harder for foreign students to enroll.

“The U.S. is committing suicide,” Yasheng Huang, a professor at M.I.T., told me, referring to the Trumpian campaign to demonize higher education and hobble cutting-edge research.

Another source of American greatness that Trump is throttling is immigration. The United States gained immensely from successive waves of newcomers from around the world, often arriving destitute and without English (like my father in 1952) but lifting their families up over a generation or two. One reason we’re a global leader in science and technology is that we’ve been able to recruit the brightest minds and hardest workers from across the globe.

When I lived in China decades ago, I was an interviewer of applicants to Harvard, and one of the students I told the university it would be lucky to have was a brilliant young woman named Sofie Qiao. She was admitted and went on to earn a Ph.D. and become an American. Today she is a serial biotechnology entrepreneur in Silicon Valley, helping develop treatments for breast and prostate cancers and for mesothelioma. She is now helping save the lives of other Americans.

Under Trump, fewer of today’s Sofies are coming to America. The number of international students arriving in August 2025 for the fall semester dropped by almost one-fifth, and the number in August 2026 fell by another 12 percent.

A third pillar that has made America the world’s leading country is the bundle of norms that govern our politics, economics and society.

Until Trump came along, I believed it was laws and the Constitution that were the country’s primary guardrails, but as I’ve seen how Trump has bullied his way past Congress and the courts, I’ve come to think that norms are just as important in underpinning democracy and economic strength. I’m thinking of simple traditions — such as that presidents will honor election results, won’t persecute rivals and will refrain from starting reckless trade wars with, well, everyone.

Norms of self-restraint historically made the system work. Presidents did not try to crush law firms or universities, nor did their administrations mislead federal courts or send armed officers into cities, where they shot people. Presidents quarreled with allies but didn’t threaten to invade Greenland.

Trump has tried to pulverize those norms by vilifying immigrants, denigrating women and threatening to “annihilate” Iran. Just this month, he called a female federal judge a “crazed lunatic.”

“The vitriol is toxic,” says David Beasley, the former Republican governor of South Carolina, “and it is undeniably feeding into the hearts, minds and souls of Americans.”

Trump is attempting to establish what feels to me like a personality cult, putting his name on the Kennedy Center and his photo on national park passes and some passports; I’m reminded of Bangladesh under its last dictator, who had herself named “mother of humanity” and put her picture and her father’s everywhere. Other presidents redecorated; Trump tore down the East Wing of the White House, is building a ballroom and aims to construct a so-called Arc de Trump.

Then there’s the greed, on a new level altogether. Trump reaped at least $2.2 billion last year, in his first year back in the White House, much of it from his family’s cryptocurrency businesses, a Times analysis found. That’s more than $6 million per day. When Amazon reportedly paid $40 million to acquire the Melania Trump documentary, I recalled covering corruption in Indonesia in the 1990s, when the wife of the president, Madame Tien, was nicknamed Madame Tien Percent.

The mix of grandiosity, authoritarianism and sleaze dribbling out of the White House is polluting government, civil society and the economy. Having spent much of my journalistic career reporting in two-bit dictatorships, I see so much that is familiar; it’s heartbreaking to see this unfold in my own country.

Trump has worked to undermine the entire international system the United States created after World War II — for our benefit and the world’s — to promote peace, trade, prosperity and health. Ebola, poverty and Vladimir Putin are beneficiaries. Imagine if in 1943 President Franklin Roosevelt had abandoned Britain and switched to back the Third Reich; that is a bit like Trump’s seeming pivot from Ukraine to Russia.

We may not have reached bottom. A particularly dangerous step would be for Trump to invoke the Insurrection Act and dispatch troops to crush protests or seize ballot boxes. Asked about the Insurrection Act, Trump told Time magazine: “I could use it. A lot of people think I should use it sometimes.”

None of this is normal. We are betraying other countries but also our own history and culture. I always wondered what citizens of ancient Rome, a proud and sophisticated empire, thought when one of their crazy emperors came to power; now I have a glimmer of understanding.

“This is the greatest heist in the history of the world: stealing America,” the singer Bono said of what has unfolded. “Everything we love is on the line,” he told me.

So those are the stakes in this election: Will we accept the loss? Or will we try to get our nation back?

The Times is committed to publishing a diversity of letters to the editor. We’d like to hear what you think about this or any of our articles. Here are some tips. And here’s our email: letters@nytimes.com.
